item.title: Can artificial intelligence align with Indigenous science?
item.dc:creator: Yvette Running Horse Collin
item.description:
Authors: Yvette Running Horse Collin
Journal: Science; Volume: 394; Issue: 6824; Pages: 575-575
Abstract: As the use of generative and agentic artificial intelligence (AI) increases, alarms are being raised about how the technology could replace human contribution, override human supervision, ignore ethical and technical guardrails, and cause increasingly irreparable harm to the environment. This creates potentially destructive outcomes for life on Earth. From a traditional Indigenous science perspective, such possibilities in themselves would be enough to immediately stop presently configured AI releases. In a Lakota context, science must ensure as little harm as possible is done to life. Therefore, AI as presently configured simply would not qualify to advance further from an ethical and scientific standpoint. Indigenous science asks something fundamentally different than what AI presently seeks to, or can, answer. But that does not mean that future forms of AI can never align with Indigenous science.

item.title: Tumor metastasis co-opts liver hematopoiesis to promote immunosuppression
item.dc:creator: Qiang Pan
Xuege Wang
Yaqi Li
Ni Li
Ying Han
Guoying Zhang
Jiacheng Guo
Le Zhang
item.description:
Authors: Qiang Pan, Xuege Wang, Yaqi Li, Ni Li, Ying Han, Guoying Zhang, Jiacheng Guo, Le Zhang, et al.
Journal: Science; Volume: 394; Issue: 6824; Article number: eaea3046
Abstract: Cancer-associated hematopoietic abnormalities contribute to systemic immunosuppression. However, whether tumors can initiate localized extramedullary hematopoiesis to suppress antitumor immunity remains unclear. In this study, we identify a distinct form of hepatic hematopoiesis driven by liver metastasis–associated hematopoietic stem cells (LM-HSCs). Liver metastases establish ectopic periportal hematopoietic niches that recruit bone marrow HSCs through Kupffer cell–dependent C-C motif chemokine receptor 1 (CCR1) signaling. Although LM-HSCs retain self-renewal and multipotency, cAMP response element–binding protein (CREB) activation skews their differentiation toward the myeloid lineage, particularly annexin A1–positive (ANXA1 + ) immature neutrophils. These neutrophils produce glucocorticoids, which activate glucocorticoid receptor signaling in a paracrine manner and induce immune checkpoint receptor expression and functional anergy in CD8 + T and natural killer cells. Collectively, these findings suggest that liver metastases reprograms hepatic hematopoiesis to promote immunosuppression.

item.title: Discovering molecular modulators with nanoswitch screening
item.dc:creator: Clinton H. Hansen
Mark Lipstein
Sarah C. Erlandson
Tobias Schwalbe
Sylvie G. Bernier
Peter Gmeiner
Andrew C. Kruse
Wesley P. Wong
item.description:
Authors: Clinton H. Hansen, Mark Lipstein, Sarah C. Erlandson, Tobias Schwalbe, Sylvie G. Bernier, Peter Gmeiner, Andrew C. Kruse, Wesley P. Wong
Journal: Science; Volume: 394; Issue: 6824; Article number: eadt7185
Abstract: Molecules that modulate protein-protein interactions, including through ternary complex formation, have been established as key therapeutics. Yet they can be challenging to discover, as standard screening approaches often lack throughput or fail to directly assay multibody interactions. We addressed this by combining DNA nanoswitch–based selection of nucleotide-encoded libraries with next-generation sequencing to create FIND (Functional Interaction–based Nanoswitch Discovery), which enables ultrahigh-throughput discovery of compounds that induce or increase protein-protein interactions. We demonstrate FIND by discovering nanobodies that stabilize the interaction between angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 and the receptor-binding domain of severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 and by discovering agonists of peroxisome proliferator–activated receptor gamma from a DNA-barcoded small-molecule library. By enabling rapid discovery of molecular modulators, FIND could lead to new therapeutics across many conditions.

item.title: Quantum gas microscopy of three-flavor Hubbard systems
item.dc:creator: Jirayu Mongkolkiattichai
Liyu Liu
Sohail Dasgupta
Kaden R. A. Hazzard
Peter Schauss
item.description:
Authors: Jirayu Mongkolkiattichai, Liyu Liu, Sohail Dasgupta, Kaden R. A. Hazzard, Peter Schauss
Journal: Science; Volume: 394; Issue: 6824; Pages: 665-669
Abstract: Hubbard systems are paradigmatic realizations of strongly correlated many-body systems. Introducing additional species breaks the SU(2) symmetry of the Hubbard model and leads to a wide variety of new exotic quantum phases. Here, we extended quantum gas microscopy to three-flavor Fermi lattice gases in the Hubbard regime. Relying on site- and flavor-resolved detection, we studied the phase diagram of the three-flavor Hubbard model and found signatures of flavor-selective localization and selective pairing at temperatures down to the tunneling energy scale. Our measurements were then compared with numerical linked-cluster expansion calculations. Further increase of phase space density may enable the observation of a distinct pair Mott phase at half filling and shows a path toward the study of color superfluidity and other aspects of quantum chromodynamics.

item.title: Targeting hormone conversion through dietary fiber improves polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome
item.dc:creator: Xinyu Qi
Hong Chen
Qixing Nie
Hongyu Niu
Yong Ding
Xi Luo
Manfei Si
Shuqi Wu
item.description:
Authors: Xinyu Qi, Hong Chen, Qixing Nie, Hongyu Niu, Yong Ding, Xi Luo, Manfei Si, Shuqi Wu, et al.
Journal: Science; Volume: 394; Issue: 6824; Article number: eaed8952
Abstract: Excessive androgens serve as a primary driver for many phenotypic features of polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome (PMOS). Although dietary fiber has been shown to alleviate PMOS, its effects on androgen concentrations and the underlying mechanisms remain unclear. In a clinical trial, we demonstrated that a dietary fiber combination consisting of inulin, resistant starch, and β-glucan reduces androgen concentrations in patients’ plasma. Mechanistically, dietary fiber increased the abundance of Bacteroides xylanisolven s, which converts androstenedione into a nonandrogenic secondary hormone metabolite we named coproandrosterone, which is further metabolized by gut microbiota into dihydro-coproandrosterone. This metabolic pathway was validated in a mouse model. These findings highlight the potential of dietary fiber to alleviate PMOS by modulating androgen homeostasis through gut microbiota, offering insights for prebiotic and probiotic therapies.

item.title: Direct evidence for psychoactive cannabis use 2800 years ago
item.dc:creator: Gino Caspari
Timur Sadykov
Daria Fomicheva
Jegor Blochin
Dominic Armbruster
Oliver Happel
Natalia Ryabogina
Kseniia Boxleitner
item.description:
Authors: Gino Caspari, Timur Sadykov, Daria Fomicheva, Jegor Blochin, Dominic Armbruster, Oliver Happel, Natalia Ryabogina, Kseniia Boxleitner, et al.
Journal: Science; Volume: 394; Issue: 6824; Pages: 649-653
Abstract: Cannabis is the world’s most-used illicit psychoactive plant, yet direct prehistoric evidence for its consumption is rare. In this study, we present the earliest direct evidence of cannabis use: offerings of plant parts and chemical compounds in ancient human hair recovered from a monumental tomb in Siberia. The findings suggest that the plant was used for its psychoactive qualities across Eurasia, where specific wild populations might have had naturally higher active compound levels. We show that the practice of cannabis consumption dates back at least 2800 years, anchoring debates around contemporary usage and informing discussions on cannabis in medicine, public health, law, and industry.

item.title: Obesity pharmacotherapies and cognition
item.dc:creator: Stina Börchers
Giulia Mazzini
Henrik Zetterberg
Christoffer Clemmensen
item.description:
Authors: Stina Börchers, Giulia Mazzini, Henrik Zetterberg, Christoffer Clemmensen
Journal: Science; Volume: 394; Issue: 6824; Pages: 633-640
Abstract: Pharmacotherapies for obesity and type 2 diabetes are increasingly being evaluated for their effects on cognition and brain health. Evidence from preclinical models, observational cohorts, and clinical trials has intensified interest, but findings remain mixed. A central challenge is to determine whether potential cognitive effects arise from direct actions on neural circuits, indirect consequences of improved cardiometabolic health, or both. This Review examines the evidence across cardiometabolic disease, aging, and Alzheimer’s disease, focusing on glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1)–based therapies and combination approaches that engage glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide, glucagon, and amylin pathways. We assess how receptor pharmacology, brain exposure, metabolic context, and disease stage shape cognitive outcomes and discuss how mechanistic clarity could guide therapies aimed at preserving or improving cognition.

item.title: Quantum gases below 10 picokelvin in space
item.dc:creator: Wei Xiong
Tang Li
Shengjie Jin
Qi Huang
Bin Wang
Lin Li
Yufeng He
Xiaopeng Li
item.description:
Authors: Wei Xiong, Tang Li, Shengjie Jin, Qi Huang, Bin Wang, Lin Li, Yufeng He, Xiaopeng Li, et al.
Journal: Science; Article number: eaea5324
Abstract: Ultracold atom platforms enable low temperatures and long free evolution times, which are crucial for fundamental physics tests and atom interferometry. The lowest equivalent temperature reported in such a system is 38 pK with a free expansion time of 2 s, achieved in atom-chip-based magnetic traps in microgravity. Optical dipole trap (ODT) systems offer better optical access and the flexibility to condense both magnetic and non-magnetic atoms, but have not been used to prepare quantum degenerate gases under microgravity conditions. Here we report an ODT-based Bose-Einstein condensate created aboard the China Space Station, containing 2.0 × 10 4 atoms, reaching an equivalent temperature of 9.7 − 2.7 + 3.2 pK with a free expansion time of 7.0 s. This record-low temperature could stimulate a new generation of ODT-based experiments in quantum simulation and precision measurements in space.

item.title: The first 1000 days: Modeling language learning from individual children’s everyday speech
item.dc:creator: Hadas Raviv
Arkadii Tsyhanov
Kira Gousios
Aja Altenhof
Haocheng Wang
Berlin Chen
Ofri Raviv
Tal Rosenwein
item.description:
Authors: Hadas Raviv, Arkadii Tsyhanov, Kira Gousios, Aja Altenhof, Haocheng Wang, Berlin Chen, Ofri Raviv, Tal Rosenwein, et al.
Journal: Science; Volume: 394; Issue: 6824; Article number: eaeh9311
Abstract: Children learn to understand and speak from the speech around them, yet how that everyday input shapes learning remains unresolved. Large language models show that language is learnable from data, but their scale and training conditions differ sharply from a child’s natural experience. We trained cognitively feasible, child-specific models on longitudinal home recordings from eight children across their first 1000 days of life. Each model learned incrementally from a single child’s ordered speech input without prior linguistic knowledge, developing phoneme-like and word-form representations that tracked each child’s learning pace. Learning was dependent on dense daily sampling and replay of recent input, indicating that both experience- and memory-related processes are necessary. These findings show that everyday experience contains sufficient structure for language learning and establish child-specific modeling for testing developmental theories.

item.title: Equivalence of pseudogap and pairing energy in a cuprate high-temperature superconductor
item.dc:creator: Jiasen Niu
Maialen Ortego Larrazabal
Thomas Gozlinski
Yudai Sato
Koen M. Bastiaans
Tjerk Benschop
Jian-Feng Ge
Yaroslav M. Blanter
item.description:
Authors: Jiasen Niu, Maialen Ortego Larrazabal, Thomas Gozlinski, Yudai Sato, Koen M. Bastiaans, Tjerk Benschop, Jian-Feng Ge, Yaroslav M. Blanter, et al.
Journal: Science; Volume: 394; Issue: 6824; Pages: 682-685
Abstract: The pseudogap stands out in the phase diagram of the cuprate high-temperature superconductors because its origin and relationship to superconductivity remain elusive. The origin of the pseudogap has been debated, with competing hypotheses attributing it to preformed electron pairs or local order, such as charge density waves. We present unambiguous evidence supporting the pairing scenario, using local shot-noise spectroscopy measurements in Bi 2 Sr 2 CaCu 2 O 8+δ . Our data demonstrate that the pseudogap energy coincides with the onset of electron pairing and is spatially heterogeneous with values reaching up to 70 milli–electron volts. Our results exclude a pure local order origin of the pseudogap, link the pseudogap to Cooper pair formation, and suggest that the limiting factor for higher critical temperature in cuprates is phase coherence.

item.title: Denoising the US Census: Succinct block hierarchical regression
item.dc:creator: Badih Ghazi
Pritish Kamath
Ravi Kumar
Pasin Manurangsi
Adam Sealfon*
item.description:
Authors: Badih Ghazi, Pritish Kamath, Ravi Kumar, Pasin Manurangsi, Adam Sealfon*
Journal: Science; Volume: 394; Issue: 6824; Pages: 686-692
Abstract: The 2020 United States Census adopted differential privacy to protect individual confidentiality, adding calibrated noise to summary demographic measurements that are then reconciled into population tables. We developed BlueDown, a postprocessing algorithm that combines techniques from linear regression and constrained optimization while exploiting measurement structure for efficiency. On 2020 Census data, BlueDown reduced the error of groupings by race at the county level by 21 to 36% and of all county-level groupings by 9 to 58%; at the tract level, it reduced error of groupings by housing type by 38 to 61%. These gains came at no cost to confidentiality or computational efficiency and would improve the validity of research relying on this definitive dataset and analyses used to guide the distribution of more than $1.5 trillion in annual federal spending.

item.title: Echoes of the Anthropocene: Noise pollution as a global threat
item.dc:creator: Hansjoerg P. Kunc
Rouven Schmidt
item.description:
Authors: Hansjoerg P. Kunc, Rouven Schmidt
Journal: Science; Volume: 394; Issue: 6824; Pages: 660-664
Abstract: Anthropogenic noise is a rapidly expanding global pollutant, but its effects across biological levels from individuals to ecosystems remain unquantified. We conducted phylogenetically controlled meta-analyses of 214 experimental studies on 177 aquatic and terrestrial species with ranges that span six continents. Noise altered at least one physiological, developmental, or behavioral trait in 80% of species studied, with declines in fitness and abundance and disruptions of predator-prey interactions. Effects occurred in every habitat, although response mechanisms varied for some traits and species, creating winners and losers. Only multispecies analyses can reveal such species- and ecosystem-level impacts of anthropogenic stressors. Our results establish noise as a novel selection pressure reshaping ecosystem dynamics and as a pervasive stressor requiring soundscape protection alongside habitat conservation.

item.title: Stacked porous NiTi structure with low cost and ultrahigh fatigue life for elastocaloric cooling
item.dc:creator: Changfeng Su
Yang Li
Zhongzheng Deng
Shiyu Zhong
Jiyuan Hu
Xueshi Li
Qiao Li
Qingping Sun
item.description:
Authors: Changfeng Su, Yang Li, Zhongzheng Deng, Shiyu Zhong, Jiyuan Hu, Xueshi Li, Qiao Li, Qingping Sun
Journal: Science; Volume: 394; Issue: 6824; Pages: 670-675
Abstract: Elastocaloric cooling (eC) uses shape memory alloys (SMAs) as energy-efficient, eco-friendly refrigerants. However, cost-effectively fabricating SMAs into fatigue-resistant, heat transfer–enhanced structures remains a key obstacle to commercialization of the eC technology. We introduce a “stamping and stacking” (S-S) method for producing porous, fatigue-resistant SMA structures. Honeycomb-like chips are stamped from nitinol (NiTi) thin sheets and then stacked into a layered tubular structure to increase heat exchange surface and at the same time avoid buckling and splitting failures encountered in existing SMA structures. The stacked structure endures >10 8 compression cycles and can deliver high specific cooling power of 3850 watts per kilogram. Our S-S method reduces fabrication costs by one order of magnitude compared with existing approaches, enabling mass production of eC refrigerant structures for commercial deployment.

item.title: Seafloor geodesy delineates fast megathrust relocking after the giant 2011 Tohoku earthquake
item.dc:creator: Fumiaki Tomita
Tianhaozhe Sun
Motoyuki Kido
Takeshi Iinuma
Naoki Uchida
Yusaku Ohta
Ryota Hino
Jiangheng He
item.description:
Authors: Fumiaki Tomita, Tianhaozhe Sun, Motoyuki Kido, Takeshi Iinuma, Naoki Uchida, Yusaku Ohta, Ryota Hino, Jiangheng He, et al.
Journal: Science; Volume: 394; Issue: 6824; Pages: 676-681
Abstract: How and when the subduction megathrust recovers its locking state after a great earthquake is important to understanding earthquake-cycle physics and future hazards. Here we report the delineation of the relocking process after the 2011 magnitude 9 Tohoku earthquake with 14 years of postseismic seafloor geodetic observations. These data, combined with onshore geodetic observations, analyses of repeating earthquakes, and numerical modeling, reveal how the recovery of locking is interrupted by afterslip on the megathrust and accompanied by stress relaxation in the viscoelastic upper mantle. The results indicate that the megathrust has already arrived at a locking state today similar to that before the earthquake despite the ongoing stress relaxation. The acquired knowledge aids understanding of megathrust earthquake cycles at other subduction zones.

item.title: Obesity management medications: The way forward
item.dc:creator: Matthias Blüher
item.description:
Authors: Matthias Blüher
Journal: Science; Volume: 394; Issue: 6824; Pages: 626-632
Abstract: Obesity is now widely recognized as a chronic progressive condition. The altered biological mechanisms that cause obesity frequently require long-term treatment, including pharmacotherapies or bariatric surgery. In recent decades, the pathophysiology of obesity has been understood to an extent that obesity management medication (OMM) discovery could be rationally pursued. Advances in defining the regulation of food intake and energy expenditure by molecular communication from peripheral organs to the brain led to the development of OMMs that appear capable of safely achieving scalable and sustained body weight loss. However, side effects, heterogeneous treatment responses, long-term metabolic adaptations, adherence, and other factors may limit the use of existing OMMs and justify the development of additional medications to improve the health of people living with obesity.

item.title: Glacial abrupt transitions in ocean circulation were much slower than ice-core records imply
item.dc:creator: Xiyu Dong
Xu Zhang
Yuchen Sun
Gayatri Kathayat
Youwei Li
Sune O. Rasmussen
Anders Svensson
Christo Buizert
item.description:
Authors: Xiyu Dong, Xu Zhang, Yuchen Sun, Gayatri Kathayat, Youwei Li, Sune O. Rasmussen, Anders Svensson, Christo Buizert, et al.
Journal: Science; Volume: 394; Issue: 6824; Pages: 654-659
Abstract: Dansgaard-Oeschger (DO) events during the last ice age are thought to reflect rapid shifts in the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC). Greenland ice cores suggest warming transitions within only a few decades—or even just over 10 years. Using precisely dated speleothem oxygen-isotope records from the Asian monsoon region, we have shown that the same DO warmings unfolded over more than a century. Isotope modeling revealed that Greenland records primarily capture a rapid atmospheric reorganization triggered by the initial sea-ice retreat in the northeastern North Atlantic, whereas the parallel AMOC recovery and hemispheric thermal adjustment proceeded much more slowly. These findings reveal that natural AMOC transitions evolved more slowly than the rapid North Greenland oxygen-isotope shifts would imply, thereby refining our understanding of “abruptness” during DO events.

item.title: When fat adapts: From physiological remodeling to disease
item.dc:creator: Karima Drareni
Patrick Seale
item.description:
Authors: Karima Drareni, Patrick Seale
Journal: Science; Volume: 394; Issue: 6824; Pages: 618-625
Abstract: Adipose tissue undergoes extensive remodeling to adapt to changing physiological demands. This plasticity encompasses changes in adipocyte metabolism and number, extracellular matrix organization, vascularization, immune composition, and innervation. When coordinated, these processes preserve energy buffering, thermogenesis, endocrine function, and local tissue support. Pathological adipose tissue remodeling drives obesity-related complications and contributes to many diseases involving organ-associated adipose depots throughout the body. In cancer, tumor-associated fat can develop a metabolic and fibroinflammatory niche that promotes tumor growth and invasion, and remodeling of other depots can directly disrupt neighboring tissues. Recent studies have identified mesenchymal, immune, vascular, and adipocyte states that govern adaptive or pathological outcomes. These findings broaden therapeutic goals beyond reducing fat mass toward restoring adipogenesis, substrate turnover, thermogenic capacity, and tissue-niche function.

item.title: The global geography of threats to freshwater biodiversity
item.dc:creator: Christophe Brabant
Laura Pollock
Jonas Geldmann
Mette Bendixen
Lise Comte
Harith Farooq
Katherine Hébert
Bernhard Lehner
item.description:
Authors: Christophe Brabant, Laura Pollock, Jonas Geldmann, Mette Bendixen, Lise Comte, Harith Farooq, Katherine Hébert, Bernhard Lehner, et al.
Journal: Science; Volume: 394; Issue: 6823; Pages: 510-514
Abstract: Human activities are eroding biodiversity, especially in freshwater systems. Despite major advances in quantifying species vulnerability and threats, we still lack a crucial understanding of where threats are affecting freshwater species globally. Here, we produced a species-centered spatial assessment of threats, mapping the impact of 45 threats across 21,490 freshwater species of amphibians, fish, mammals, odonates, and reptiles. We found that species in highly developed and water-managed regions are strongly affected by multiple overlapping threats. Although threats vary across taxa and regions, increasing threat probabilities elevate extinction risk and population declines, with freshwater species experiencing greater threat intensity and distinct spatial patterns than terrestrial species. Our findings establish a spatially explicit baseline for targeting the most urgently needed freshwater conservation and management interventions.

item.dc:creator: Kazuo Okanoya

item.title: Data-driven discovery and rapid, direct synthesis of MXenes
item.dc:creator: Ali Saffar Shamshirgar
Guilherme Ribeiro Portugal
Soheil Ershadrad
Roman Ivanov
Martin Dahlqvist
Florian Chabanais
Sanjay Chakraborty

item.description:
Authors: Ali Saffar Shamshirgar, Guilherme Ribeiro Portugal, Soheil Ershadrad, Roman Ivanov, Martin Dahlqvist, Florian Chabanais, Sanjay Chakraborty, Rainer Traksmaa, et al.
Journal: Science; Volume: 394; Issue: 6823; Article number: eaeh5957
Abstract: MXenes are a rapidly expanding family of two-dimensional transition metal carbides and nitrides, yet scalable synthesis routes remain limited and historical reports suggest a broader, largely unexplored chemical space. We used machine learning–assisted database mining to uncover hidden multilayer MXenes. Screening reveals 33 previously synthesized but unrecognized MXene candidates. Guided by these findings, we synthesized seven multilayer MXenes using a rapid, scalable self-propagating high-temperature method that requires no sustained external heating and completes within minutes. We further realized 11 previously unexplored rare earth–based MXenes (M = praseodymium, neodymium, samarium, gadolinium, terbium, holmium, and thulium). Experiments and modeling suggest semiconducting behavior and diverse magnetic states across this family. Together, these results expand the MXene family and demonstrate a data-driven strategy for accelerating materials discovery through sustainable methods.

item.title: A commensally regulated immune rheostat fine-tunes skin barrier fitness
item.dc:creator: Anita Gola
Rohith Srinivas
Elias G. Rodig
Marina Schernthanner
Merve Deniz Abdusselamoglu
Matthew T. Tierney
Natalie J. Alexander

item.description:
Authors: Anita Gola, Rohith Srinivas, Elias G. Rodig, Marina Schernthanner, Merve Deniz Abdusselamoglu, Matthew T. Tierney, Natalie J. Alexander, Kevin A. U. Gonzales, et al.
Journal: Science; Volume: 394; Issue: 6823; Article number: eaee5920
Abstract: At the skin’s surface, the epidermis must balance stem cell renewal with barrier maintenance to withstand environmental stress and shield against pathogens. In this study, we identify a microbial-immune-epithelial feedback mechanism that integrates environmental information into stem cell regulation in mice. Specifically, we show that Langerhans cells (LCs), an intraepithelial macrophage population, orchestrate this circuit by producing prostaglandin E 2 , which restrains stem cell proliferation, promotes epidermal differentiation, and maintains barrier integrity during homeostasis. Upon pathway disruption, stem cells become overactivated, hindering terminal differentiation and weakening barrier function. Upstream, LC activity is tuned by the local microbial environment in a rheostat-like fashion, coupling commensal sensing to stem cell dynamics. Our findings provide a general framework for how barrier tissues achieve adaptive homeostasis amid continual external fluctuations.

item.title: Intrinsic gestational timing governs human cerebellar development after preterm birth
item.dc:creator: Georgios Sanidas
Gabriele Simonti
Javid Ghaemmaghami
Kyla Woyshner
Antonis Polyviou
Robinson Vidva
Courtney Lowe
Abhya Vij
item.description:
Authors: Georgios Sanidas, Gabriele Simonti, Javid Ghaemmaghami, Kyla Woyshner, Antonis Polyviou, Robinson Vidva, Courtney Lowe, Abhya Vij, et al.
Journal: Science; Volume: 394; Issue: 6823; Pages: 549-555
Abstract: Intrinsic programs shape brain maturation; however, which of these programs are perturbed by prematurity as well as the molecular pathways involved remain unknown. The human cerebellum serves as a paradigm of extrauterine development—its accelerated growth and circuit formation align with the third trimester, a period disrupted by preterm delivery. Using multimodal datasets encompassing in vivo neuroimaging and neurodevelopmental outcomes with postmortem spatial-transcriptomic and histopathological profiling, we show that prematurity diverts the cerebellar developmental trajectory. Cerebellar growth and functional outcomes scaled with gestational age, despite modifying perinatal exposures. Spatially resolved developmental programs underlying macroscopic trajectories were marked by incomplete granule cell maturation and impaired Purkinje cell structural refinement, which indicate lineage-specific developmental asynchrony. Thus, prematurity constitutes biologically displaced maturation, in which infants of equivalent postmenstrual age occupy divergent developmental states.

item.title: Pervasive patterns in bird songs resemble those in human speech and song and are independent of vocal learning
item.dc:creator: Logan S. James
Kendra Oudyk
Maria I. Pescaru
Erin M. Wall
Yining Chen
William D. Pearse
Jon T. Sakata
item.description:
Authors: Logan S. James, Kendra Oudyk, Maria I. Pescaru, Erin M. Wall, Yining Chen, William D. Pearse, Jon T. Sakata
Journal: Science; Volume: 394; Issue: 6823; Pages: 556-561
Abstract: Bird songs are often described as analogs to human speech and songs, but expansive comparisons are necessary to determine analogy and mechanistic substrates. By analyzing global corpora consisting of 367 bird species (>74,500 vocal elements from ~5900 songs) within two clades of vocal learners (oscines and hummingbirds) and related nonlearners (suboscines and nightjars) and 52 human languages (>15,000 elements in >800 speech or song phrases), we revealed common patterns in bird songs that resemble prevalent patterns in human speech and song with variation in resemblance to speech or song. Vocal learning did not systematically affect acoustic patterning or similarity to human vocalizations. These data underscore the deep analogies between bird and human vocalizations and convergent motor mechanisms shaping communication.

item.title: The delocalized nature of chemical bonding at a catalytic metal surface
item.dc:creator: Florian Nitz
Stefan Hörandl
Jonathan Pätzold
Alexander Kandratsenka
Theofanis N. Kitsopoulos
Daniel J. Auerbach
Alec M. Wodtke
Dmitriy Borodin
item.description:
Authors: Florian Nitz, Stefan Hörandl, Jonathan Pätzold, Alexander Kandratsenka, Theofanis N. Kitsopoulos, Daniel J. Auerbach, Alec M. Wodtke, Dmitriy Borodin
Journal: Science; Volume: 394; Issue: 6823; Pages: 529-533
Abstract: Adsorbate bonding at metal surfaces requires hybridization of localized molecular orbitals with delocalized electronic bands of the metal; hence, the electronic wave function involved in bonding may extend far beyond the adsorption site. We revealed the consequence of this delocalization by determining the distance over which structural variations of the metal surface influence the molecule-metal bond strength. Velocity-resolved kinetics provided adsorption energies for three molecules bound at atomic steps of platinum (Pt), each exhibiting bond-strength changes of up to 0.2 electron volts as the step-step distance varied over 100 angstroms. We observed molecule-specific behavior reflecting the hybridization of molecule-specific orbitals with symmetry-selected orbital bands of the metal that respond differently to structural modifications of the solid. We discuss implications of these observations for adsorption on Pt nanoparticles.

item.title: In-cell structures visualize human pre-ribosome assembly in the nucleolus
item.dc:creator: Xiaohan Zhao
Yuki Hayashi
Herman K. H. Fung
Sara Cuylen-Haering
Julia Mahamid
Christoph W. Müller
item.description:
Authors: Xiaohan Zhao, Yuki Hayashi, Herman K. H. Fung, Sara Cuylen-Haering, Julia Mahamid, Christoph W. Müller
Journal: Science; Volume: 394; Issue: 6823; Pages: 534-540
Abstract: In eukaryotes, ribosome biogenesis initiates within the nucleolus, a hallmark multilayered compartment of the nucleus. Structures of pre-ribosomes have been characterized ex situ, but their assembly pathways within human nucleoli have not been described. Here, we used cryogenic correlative light and electron tomography to visualize molecular landscapes within HeLa cell nucleoli and obtained in-cell structural snapshots of both ribosomal subunit precursors, the small subunit processome and the pre-60S. These recapitulate major states resolved previously ex situ and reveal additional critical interaction partners, including the RNA exosome, rixosome, and nuclear export receptor CRM1-RanGTP. We further show how pre-ribosome assembly landscapes are altered upon RNA polymerase I inhibition. Our study combines molecular structures with cellular context to elucidate the spatiotemporal assembly pathway of the human ribosome.

item.title: Stimulated protein degradation to promote mitochondrial function and neuronal survival
item.dc:creator: Srividya Chandrasekhar
Rachael McMinimy
Andrew G. Manford

Caitlyn Miller

John Kuriyan
item.description:
Authors: Srividya Chandrasekhar, Rachael McMinimy, Andrew G. Manford, Eddie Wehri, Christine L. Gee, Caitlyn Miller, Baris Bingol, John Kuriyan, et al.
Journal: Science; Volume: 394; Issue: 6823; Article number: eaed2525
Abstract: Targeted protein degradation is a promising modality to treat cancer or inflammation, but whether it can provide a similar benefit for disorders caused by pervasive protein dysregulation is unclear. We describe stimulated protein degradation (SPD) as a strategy that leverages agonists of stress-responsive E3 ubiquitin ligases to simultaneously eliminate multiple pathogenic factors. Specifically, we show that activators of the reductive stress response E3 CUL2 FEM1B boost degradation of multiple physiological substrates to improve mitochondrial import and electron transport chain assembly. In this manner, CUL2 FEM1B agonists preserve mitochondrial function and neuronal survival in models of neurodegenerative COX deficiency syndrome and Friedreich’s ataxia. By activating E3 ligases that evolved to safeguard cellular integrity, SPD expands the use of compound-induced protein degradation to complex pathologies of high unmet need.

item.title: Western Pacific double subduction drives Gulf of California rifting
item.dc:creator: Guido M. Gianni
Xiang He
Thorsten W. Becker
Claudio Faccenna
item.description:
Authors: Guido M. Gianni, Xiang He, Thorsten W. Becker, Claudio Faccenna
Journal: Science; Volume: 394; Issue: 6823; Pages: 515-519
Abstract: Continental rifting reflects the balance between tectonic forces and lithospheric strength, yet the mechanisms of breakup remain debated. Rapid rifting of the Gulf of California oblique rift (GOCOR) ~6 million to 8 million years ago is a key example; it may have resulted from the lithosphere responding to external kinematics or acceleration of long-lived extension. The dynamics of either scenario remain incompletely understood. In this study, we highlight that the rapid rifting of the GOCOR coincides with the initiation of Western Pacific double subduction. Using three-dimensional geodynamic models, we show that such subduction reorganization can transmit extensional stresses of ~5 to 15 megapascals across the Pacific plate, loading the GOCOR and the southern San Andreas fault. Subduction reorganization may represent the missing driver for the initiation of rapid GOCOR rifting within a preconditioned lithosphere and may be an overlooked tectonic force behind other rifting events.

item.description:
Authors: Yang Liu, Lee M. Saper, Elizabeth Ann Bell, Chi Ma, Haoyu Li, Jinping Hu, Yunbin Guan, Hayward Melton, et al.
Journal: Science; Article number: eadz5646
Abstract: Martian meteorites provide a record of the planet’s geological history. However, most are geologically young samples that are not representative of Mars’ surface, which is dominated by ancient rocks. We describe the Martian meteorite Teghaza 001 (Teg 001), a slowly cooled igneous rock that formed at least 4.1 billion years ago. Its composition, mineralogy, and texture are distinct from other Martian meteorites. We determine that Teg 001 is a sample of ancient crust, which formed from a geochemically distinct mantle source with primordial composition. The presence of aqueously altered minerals, combined with bulk and mineral-specific oxygen isotope measurements, indicate that Teg 001 experienced reactions with fluids enriched in 18 O, before ejection into space by an impact.

item.title: Papaver self-incompatibility is controlled by two multiallelic idiomorphs
item.dc:creator: Ke Jin
Zezhen Du
Tao Xiong
Fuyu Leng
Jian Liu
Mannan Zhang
Boyang Tian
Jianbing Hu
item.description:
Authors: Ke Jin, Zezhen Du, Tao Xiong, Fuyu Leng, Jian Liu, Mannan Zhang, Boyang Tian, Jianbing Hu, et al.
Journal: Science; Volume: 394; Issue: 6823; Article number: eaeg6988
Abstract: Self-incompatibility (SI) prevents self-fertilization through highly polymorphic genetic recognition at the S locus with multiple alleles. In Papaver rhoeas , the S determinants were previously identified as PrpS and PrsS . However, we found that PrpS-PrsS was absent in many S haplotypes. In this work, we report the identification of an alternative pair of polymorphic S genes, S locus oligopeptide transporter ( SOPT ) and S locus glycine-rich protein ( SGRP ), segregating at the S locus when PrpS-PrsS is absent. SOPT and SGRP display hallmark S determinant features and confer SI when heterologously expressed in Arabidopsis thaliana . Therefore, instead of having allelomorphs with homologous variants, the Papaver SI system is determined by two multiallelic idiomorphs sharing no obvious common ancestry. This discovery of a dual-idiomorph system reveals a distinct genetic basis for polymorphism, with implications for the evolution of allorecognition mechanisms.

item.title: Chiral altermagnon in MnTe
item.dc:creator: Daniel Jost
Resham Babu Regmi
Eder G. Lomeli
Samuel Sahel-Schackis
Monika Scheufele
Marcel Neuhaus
Rachel Nickel
Flora Yakhou
item.description:
Authors: Daniel Jost, Resham Babu Regmi, Eder G. Lomeli, Samuel Sahel-Schackis, Monika Scheufele, Marcel Neuhaus, Rachel Nickel, Flora Yakhou, et al.
Journal: Science; Volume: 394; Issue: 6823; Pages: 541-543
Abstract: Altermagnetism has been recognized as a magnetic phase that bridges the properties of ferro- and antiferromagnetism. The momentum-dependent spin splitting observed in these materials reflects their distinctive symmetry characteristics, which also establish the conditions for chiral magnons to emerge. Here we provide direct experimental evidence for a chiral magnon in the altermagnetic candidate manganese telluride (MnTe) revealed by circular-dichroism resonant inelastic x-ray scattering. This mode, which we term chiral altermagnon, exhibits a distinct momentum dependence of its spin polarization consistent with the altermagnetic g -wave symmetry of MnTe. Our polarization-resolved data corroborate the existence of a discrete class of magnetic excitations, demonstrating how altermagnetic order shapes spin dynamics and paving the way for advances in spintronic and quantum technologies.

item.dc:creator: Kutay Deniz Atabay
Patrick Aoude
Chanyoung Park

Olivier H. Paugois
Benjamin Judkewitz

item.description:
Authors: Kutay Deniz Atabay, Patrick Aoude, Chanyoung Park, Mykola Kadobianskyi, Olivier H. Paugois, Benjamin Judkewitz, Peter W. Reddien
Journal: Science; Volume: 394; Issue: 6823; Article number: eaeg1125
Abstract: A complete cell type transcriptome atlas of a vertebrate could promote understanding of animal cell type composition, organization, and evolution. The miniaturized, transparent, and regenerative teleost Danionella cerebrum brings whole-vertebrate single-cell profiling experiments within reach. We performed region-stratified single-cell RNA sequencing across the adult Danionella body and mapped cell types and gene expression at single-cell resolution using spatial transcriptomics. We delineated spatially distinct neural cell types on the basis of their regional gene expression signatures. The body-wide atlas elucidated cell types harboring adult molecular positional memory, uncovered paedomorphic features, and revealed conserved body-region and appendage-specification programs in adult connective tissue. Comparative analyses revealed conserved neural cell types, and regeneration datasets uncovered expression dynamics during telencephalon regeneration. This whole-vertebrate transcriptome atlas yields a comprehensive resource for myriad questions in biology and neuroscience.

item.title: Genomic erosion across avifauna in a biodiversity hotspot sounds a conservation alarm
item.dc:creator: Ri Liu
Yadan Liu
Fei Wu
Dao Yan
Feng Dong
item.description:
Authors: Ri Liu, Yadan Liu, Fei Wu, Dao Yan, Feng Dong
Journal: Science; Volume: 394; Issue: 6823; Pages: 525-528
Abstract: Loss of biodiversity can have a hidden dimension—the cryptic erosion of genetic diversity even in the face of apparent species resilience. We quantified changes in genetic diversity by comparing historical and modern genomes of 62 songbird species from the Gaoligong Mountains, a biodiversity hotspot in southwestern China. We identified genomic loss averaging between 43 and 49%; and, unexpectedly, common species were disproportionately affected. We argue that this loss was driven primarily by habitat fragmentation (and mitigated by dispersal ability) and show that it exceeds prior estimates and conservation policy thresholds. Species identified as having lost diversity continue to be listed as “Least Concern” on the International Union for Conservation of Nature’s Red List of Threatened Species, exposing a blind spot in extinction risk monitoring. We call for genomic metrics to be rapidly integrated into global conservation frameworks.

item.title: Emergence of Chern metal in a moiré Kondo lattice
item.dc:creator: Wenjin Zhao
Zui Tao
Yichi Zhang
Bowen Shen
Zhongdong Han
Patrick Knüppel
Yihang Zeng
Zhengchao Xia
item.description:
Authors: Wenjin Zhao, Zui Tao, Yichi Zhang, Bowen Shen, Zhongdong Han, Patrick Knüppel, Yihang Zeng, Zhengchao Xia, et al.
Journal: Science; Article number: eadv9181
Abstract: A Chern metal is a two-dimensional metallic state of matter carrying chiral edge states. We report the observation of a Chern metal at the onset of the magnetic Kondo breakdown in a frustrated moiré Kondo lattice--angle-aligned MoTe 2 /WSe 2 bilayers. The state is compressible and is manifested by a nearly quantized Hall resistance and a finite longitudinal resistance arising from a bad metallic bulk. We demonstrate the presence of a chiral edge state by nonlocal transport measurements and current-induced quantum anomalous Hall breakdown. Magnetic circular dichroism measurements further reveal a magnetization plateau for the Chern metal before a metamagnetic transition at the Kondo breakdown. Our results open an opportunity for moiré engineering of exotic quantum phases through the interplay between band topology and Kondo interactions.

item.title: Spatial coordination in the codevelopment of the human urogenital system during organogenesis
item.dc:creator: Yifei Guo
Hui Cai
Duan Li
Pengcheng Ren

item.description:
Authors: Yifei Guo, Hui Cai, Duan Li, Pengcheng Ren, Lina Cui, Cuifang Hao, Hui Jiang, Zhe Zhang, et al.
Journal: Science; Volume: 394; Issue: 6823; Article number: eaee5093
Abstract: The human urogenital system originates from a common embryonic domain, yet the mechanisms guiding its spatiotemporal coordination remain understudied. Here, we combined high-resolution spatial transcriptomics with single-cell multiomics to profile human embryos from Carnegie stages 15 to 23, capturing the codevelopmental dynamics of the urogenital system. We revealed mesonephros- and adrenal primordium–derived signals that promote gonadal specification and enable efficient in vitro generation of cells resembling early gonadal lineages. We also uncovered a possible mesonephric origin of gonadal supporting cells through rete testis or ovarii linking the mesonephros. Finally, we delineate three transcriptionally distinct steroidogenic lineages differing in cholesterol sourcing, cortisol synthesis, and sex hormone production that together orchestrate sex differentiation. These findings deepen our understanding of urogenital system assembly and guide the exploration of coordinated multiorgan development.

item.title: Rapid longitudinal flights cause time shifts and Sun compass error
item.dc:creator: Patrick Lewin
Joe Wynn
Joe Morford
Oliver Padget
Lewis Lancaster-Reeves
Katrina Siddiqi-Davies
Hector Bailey
Sarah Bond
item.description:
Authors: Patrick Lewin, Joe Wynn, Joe Morford, Oliver Padget, Lewis Lancaster-Reeves, Katrina Siddiqi-Davies, Hector Bailey, Sarah Bond, et al.
Journal: Science; Volume: 394; Issue: 6823; Pages: 520-524
Abstract: Many animals use the Sun compass to guide their movement, sometimes over thousands of kilometers. Consistent use of the Sun compass relies on the endogenous clock to track the Sun’s arc, yet animals traveling east-west experience time shifts, potentially causing mismatches between their internal clock and local time. Using GPS, we reveal that Manx shearwaters ( Puffinus puffinus ) experience such shifts during homing flights, generating predictable errors in Sun compass orientation. Use of the Sun compass persists even when shearwaters have access to compass-independent cues during coast following. Our findings provide a new avenue for chronobiology research in the wild, suggesting that rapid longitudinal movements may affect other processes governed by the endogenous clock and that conserved chronobiological mechanisms impose substantial constraints on navigation.

item.title: When AI takes away the thrill of discovery
item.dc:creator: H. Holden Thorp
item.description:
Authors: H. Holden Thorp
Journal: Science; Volume: 394; Issue: 6823; Pages: 471-471
Abstract: “Pure math is being devastated or revolutionized, depending on your point of view.” So said Cornell professor Steven Strogatz after the artificial intelligence (AI) company OpenAI announced in early September a potential solution to the Navier-Stokes existence and smoothness problem, one of the seven Millennium Prize problems that represent the highest goals for mathematical proofs. OpenAI’s solution involved unleashing an army of AI agents at a cost of millions of dollars in computing power, and it also certainly drew on decades of human effort in mathematics before it. Then a few weeks later, OpenAI posted 722 manuscripts describing progress on 372 mathematical problem families, and Google DeepMind published (in Science ) solutions from their own AI math system. These events are potentially exciting for those who long to know the answers to these problems as soon as possible, but they have also sent the world of mathematics reeling, and pose an even bigger question for all fields: Can the satisfaction of understanding ever replace the thrill of discovery?

item.description:
Authors: Quentin Faure, Dalila Bounoua, Victor Balédent, Arsen Gukasov, V. Ovidiu Garlea, Afonso Ribeiro, Jeffrey G. Rau, Sylvain Petit, et al.
Journal: Science; Volume: 394; Issue: 6823; Pages: 544-548
Abstract: Altermagnets are compensated magnets with symmetry-enforced spin split bands. Direct spectroscopic evidence for their existence has been reported in several materials. For example, inelastic neutron scattering (INS) has recently been used to witness a splitting of magnon bands in MnTe that is compatible with altermagnetism. Here, we present polarized INS results on MnF 2 showing that it is altermagnetic. Our data reveal a splitting coming from the long-range dipolar coupling. Furthermore, using a domain-biased sample, the data reveal a nonzero chirality in the neutron scattering cross section that reverses the sign between the two magnon modes. It is this feature that clearly demonstrates altermagnetism in MnF 2 . This finding highlights the potential for polarized INS to characterize altermagnets through its sensitivity to fine structure in magnon spectra.

item.title: Wireless electrocatalytic closed-loop system for drug-free management of diabesity
item.dc:creator: Debasis Maity
Preetam Guha Ray
Peter Buchmann
Ghislaine Charpin-El Hamri
Martin Fussenegger
item.description:
Authors: Debasis Maity, Preetam Guha Ray, Peter Buchmann, Ghislaine Charpin-El Hamri, Martin Fussenegger
Journal: Science; Volume: 394; Issue: 6822; Article number: eady8560
Abstract: Lifestyle-related type 2 diabetes and associated obesity (diabesity) affect >2.5 billion people worldwide and impose nearly $3 trillion in annual health care costs. We developed an implantable, wirelessly powered electrocatalytic closed-loop health optimization (ECHO) device containing platinum-decorated gold nanoclusters embedded in graphite felt that enabled selective, electrically tunable oxidation of blood glucose to renally cleared gluconate. In type 2 diabetic mice, wireless, low-power activation (0.75 volts, 10 milliamperes) restored glucose homeostasis within 1 hour, shifted metabolism from glucose to lipid utilization, reduced body weight and triglycerides, and increased circulating free fatty acids and ketone bodies without detectable hypoglycemia or adverse physiological, inflammatory, or behavioral effects during 6 weeks of treatment. Coupling this ECHO device to a commercial continuous glucose monitoring system enabled autonomous, smartphone-controlled, drug-free closed-loop management of experimental diabesity.

item.title: The Virtual Biotech: A multi-agent AI framework for therapeutic discovery and development
item.dc:creator: Harrison G. Zhang
Peter Eckmann
Jiacheng Miao
Andrew B. Mahon
James Zou
item.description:
Authors: Harrison G. Zhang, Peter Eckmann, Jiacheng Miao, Andrew B. Mahon, James Zou
Journal: Science; Volume: 394; Issue: 6822; Article number: eaeg6779
Abstract: Drug development requires evidence integration across biological scales and modalities, but relevant tools are fragmented. We introduce the Virtual Biotech, an organization of artificial intelligence (AI) agents modeled on a drug-development company, with agentic divisions spanning target discovery, safety assessment, modality selection, and clinical development. We demonstrate its utility at three drug-development decision points. First, more than 37,000 agents annotated outcomes from 55,984 trials and found that drugs targeting cell type–specific genes were 48% more likely to reach market with 32% fewer adverse events. Second, it integrated multimodal evidence to propose a therapeutic strategy in lung cancer. Third, it analyzed a terminated ulcerative colitis trial and inferred potential mechanisms of failure. These results demonstrate that human-guided multi-agent systems can conduct transparent, multiscale analyses to inform therapeutic-development decisions.

item.title: Thermodynamic origin of the phonon Hall effect in a honeycomb antiferromagnet
item.dc:creator: Qingkai Meng
Xiaokang Li
Jie Liu
Lingxiao Zhao
Chao Dong
Zengwei Zhu
Liang Li
Kamran Behnia
item.description:
Authors: Qingkai Meng, Xiaokang Li, Jie Liu, Lingxiao Zhao, Chao Dong, Zengwei Zhu, Liang Li, Kamran Behnia
Journal: Science; Volume: 394; Issue: 6822; Pages: 419-422
Abstract: The underlying mechanism of the thermal Hall effect generated by phonons in a variety of insulators is yet to be identified. In this work, we report on a sizable thermal Hall conductivity in nickel phosphorus trisulfide (NiPS 3 ), a van der Waals stack of honeycomb layers with a zigzag antiferromagnetic order. The longitudinal (κ aa ) and the transverse (κ ab ) thermal conductivities peak at the same temperature, and the thermal Hall angle, at this peak, respects a previously identified bound. The amplitude of κ ab is extremely sensitive to the amplitude of magnetization along the b axis but is not correlated with the phonon mean free path, which points to an intrinsic origin.

item.title: The AI debate is missing half the system
item.dc:creator: Pietro Michelucci
item.description:
Authors: Pietro Michelucci
Journal: Science; Volume: 394; Issue: 6822; Pages: 363-363
Abstract: Last month, leading executives of artificial intelligence (AI) companies warned the United Nations Security Council about the risks of losing human control over this rapidly advancing technology. Their recommendations focused heavily on safeguards, evaluation, and governance of AI models and systems, largely overlooking the risks that arise from the interactions of AI with people and institutions. AI safety needs to be addressed at the level of the human–AI system, not the AI model alone.
